answer:
Gabriel phthalimide synthesis is a method of preparing a PURE PRIMARY amine, and it is carried out in three stages.

STAGE 1 - Formation of potassium phthalimide. Phthalimide is treated with alcoholic potassium hydroxide. The hydrogen atom attached to the imide nitrogen is acidic, so it is removed and the potassium salt of phthalimide is formed.

Phthalimide \(+\ \mathrm{KOH}\) (alc.) \(\longrightarrow\) potassium phthalimide \(+\ \mathrm{H_2O}\)

STAGE 2 - Formation of N-alkylphthalimide. The potassium salt is heated with an alkyl halide \(\mathrm{R-X}\). The phthalimide anion acts as a nucleophile, displaces the halide ion and potassium halide is eliminated.

potassium phthalimide \(+\ \mathrm{R-X} \xrightarrow{\Delta}\) N-alkylphthalimide \(+\ \mathrm{KX}\)

STAGE 3 - Alkaline hydrolysis. The N-alkylphthalimide is hydrolysed with aqueous sodium hydroxide, which gives sodium phthalate together with the primary amine.

N-alkylphthalimide \(+\ 2\mathrm{NaOH(aq)} \xrightarrow{\Delta}\) sodium phthalate \(+\ \mathrm{R-NH_2}\)

The alkyl group is delivered by a nucleophilic substitution on the alkyl halide, so only ONE alkyl group can become attached to the nitrogen atom. The amine obtained is therefore a pure primary amine, free from the secondary and tertiary amines and the quaternary salt that ammonolysis of an alkyl halide produces alongside the primary amine.

LIMITATION. Aromatic amines cannot be prepared by this method, because aryl halides do not undergo nucleophilic substitution with the anion formed from phthalimide.

Hofmann bromamide degradation converts an AMIDE into a PRIMARY AMINE containing ONE CARBON ATOM LESS than the amide.

An amide is warmed with bromine and an excess of aqueous potassium hydroxide:

\(\mathrm{R-CO-NH_2} + \mathrm{Br_2} + 4\mathrm{KOH(aq)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{R-NH_2} + 2\mathrm{KBr} + \mathrm{K_2CO_3} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)

Example - acetamide gives methylamine:

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CO-NH_2} + \mathrm{Br_2} + 4\mathrm{KOH(aq)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{CH_3-NH_2} + 2\mathrm{KBr} + \mathrm{K_2CO_3} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)

Points to note:

1. The carbonyl carbon of the amide leaves as the carbonate ion, which is why the amine has one carbon atom fewer than the amide it came from. Acetamide, with two carbon atoms, therefore gives methylamine, with one.

2. The amine produced is ALWAYS a primary amine, whatever the amide, because only the nitrogen of the \(\mathrm{-CO-NH_2}\) group is carried through to the product.

3. The method is a step-DOWN of the carbon chain, and it is the reaction to choose whenever a preparation has to lose one carbon atom - the reduction of the same amide with \(\mathrm{LiAlH_4}\) would keep all the carbon atoms instead.

answer:
In Hofmann bromamide degradation an amide is treated with bromine and an excess of aqueous potassium hydroxide (or sodium hydroxide) and warmed. The product is a primary amine having ONE CARBON ATOM LESS than the amide:

\(\mathrm{R-CO-NH_2} + \mathrm{Br_2} + 4\mathrm{KOH(aq)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{R-NH_2} + 2\mathrm{KBr} + \mathrm{K_2CO_3} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)

Examples:

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CO-NH_2} + \mathrm{Br_2} + 4\mathrm{KOH(aq)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{CH_3-NH_2} + 2\mathrm{KBr} + \mathrm{K_2CO_3} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)

acetamide (2 carbon atoms) gives methylamine (1 carbon atom).

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CO-NH_2} + \mathrm{Br_2} + 4\mathrm{KOH(aq)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-NH_2} + 2\mathrm{KBr} + \mathrm{K_2CO_3} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)

propanamide (3 carbon atoms) gives ethanamine (2 carbon atoms).

Explanation of the change. The alkyl group \(\mathrm{R}\) migrates from the carbonyl carbon to the nitrogen atom, and the carbonyl carbon itself is expelled as the carbonate ion \(\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}\). That migration is why the nitrogen ends up bonded to \(\mathrm{R}\) instead of to the acyl group, and why exactly one carbon atom is lost.

Two consequences follow, and both are used in problems. First, the amine obtained is always PRIMARY. Second, the method steps the carbon chain DOWN by one, so it is the route to choose when the amine wanted has one carbon atom fewer than the starting material - the reduction of the same amide with \(\mathrm{LiAlH_4}\) keeps every carbon atom and would give a different amine.

answer:
Acetaldoxime is \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH=N-OH}\). It is reduced to ethylamine, and the oxime itself is obtained from acetaldehyde, so two reactions are involved.

STEP 1 - Formation of acetaldoxime. Acetaldehyde is treated with hydroxylamine:

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CHO} + \mathrm{NH_2OH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3-CH=N-OH} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

STEP 2 - Reduction of the oxime. The carbon-nitrogen double bond of the oxime is reduced by nascent hydrogen from sodium and ethanol, and the \(\mathrm{-OH}\) group on nitrogen is removed as water:

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH=N-OH} + 4[\mathrm{H}] \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Na/C_2H_5OH}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-NH_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

The same reduction is brought about by \(\mathrm{LiAlH_4}\) in ether, or by hydrogen over a nickel catalyst.

The product is ETHYLAMINE (ethanamine), \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-NH_2}\), a primary amine.

Checking the carbon count and the balance: the oxime \(\mathrm{C_2H_5NO}\) takes up four hydrogen atoms to give \(\mathrm{C_2H_7N}\) and \(\mathrm{H_2O}\), so both sides carry \(\mathrm{C_2H_9NO}\). The two carbon atoms of acetaldehyde are retained, so the amine has the same number of carbon atoms as the aldehyde it started from.

[Note: reduction of oximes is not one of the preparations printed in the Std XII Balbharati Amines chapter, which sets out ammonolysis, reduction of nitro compounds, reduction of nitriles, reduction of amides, Gabriel synthesis and Hofmann degradation. It was on the syllabus in force when this paper was set.]

The product is ETHYLAMINE (ethanamine), \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-NH_2}\).

Lithium aluminium hydride in dry ether is a powerful reducing agent, and it reduces the carbonyl group of an amide to a \(\mathrm{-CH_2-}\) group, leaving the nitrogen atom attached to it:

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CO-NH_2} + 4[\mathrm{H}] \xrightarrow{\mathrm{LiAlH_4/ether}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-NH_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

Acetamide is \(\mathrm{CH_3-CO-NH_2}\) and has two carbon atoms; the reduction keeps BOTH of them, so the amine formed also has two carbon atoms and is ethylamine, a primary amine.

Checking the balance: \(\mathrm{C_2H_5NO}\) with four hydrogen atoms added gives \(\mathrm{C_2H_7N}\) together with \(\mathrm{H_2O}\), and both sides carry \(\mathrm{C_2H_9NO}\).

Contrast with the other amide reaction of this chapter: treating the same acetamide with bromine and alkali (Hofmann bromamide degradation) would remove the carbonyl carbon and give methylamine. It is reduction that preserves the carbon count and gives ethylamine.

Acetamide is warmed with bromine and an excess of aqueous potassium hydroxide:

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CO-NH_2} + \mathrm{Br_2} + 4\mathrm{KOH(aq)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{CH_3-NH_2} + 2\mathrm{KBr} + \mathrm{K_2CO_3} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)

A. ACTION OF \(\mathrm{NaNO_2}\) AND DILUTE \(\mathrm{HCl}\)

Sodium nitrite with dilute hydrochloric acid generates nitrous acid \(\mathrm{HNO_2}\) in situ, because nitrous acid is itself unstable. The mixture is kept cold, at \(273\text{-}278\ \mathrm{K}\). The three amines behave differently, and that is what makes this a test.

a. ETHYLAMINE - an aliphatic PRIMARY amine. It gives an ethyl diazonium salt which is very unstable and decomposes at once by reaction with the solvent water:

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-NH_2} + \mathrm{HNO_2} \xrightarrow[(\mathrm{NaNO_2 + HCl})]{273\text{-}278\ \mathrm{K}} [\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-N_2^{\oplus}Cl^{\ominus}}] \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_2O}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-OH} + \mathrm{N_2}\uparrow + \mathrm{HCl}\)

Ethanol is formed and nitrogen gas is liberated with brisk effervescence.

b. ANILINE - an aromatic PRIMARY amine. The reaction is called diazotisation. The arene diazonium salt formed has reasonable stability at \(273\ \mathrm{K}\), so it does NOT decompose and no nitrogen is evolved:

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-NH_2} + \mathrm{HNO_2} + \mathrm{HCl} \xrightarrow{273\text{-}278\ \mathrm{K}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-N_2^{\oplus}Cl^{\ominus}} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)

The product is benzene diazonium chloride.

c. DIETHYLAMINE - a SECONDARY amine. It has only one hydrogen atom on nitrogen, so it cannot form a diazonium salt; the nitroso group attaches to the nitrogen instead and a yellow oily N-nitrosoamine separates:

\(\mathrm{(C_2H_5)_2NH} + \mathrm{HNO_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{(C_2H_5)_2N-N=O} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

The product is N-nitrosodiethylamine, a yellow oily liquid, and no gas is evolved.

B. PREPARATION OF NYLON 6,6

Nylon 6,6 is a condensation (step-growth) polymer. Hexamethylenediamine (hexane-1,6-diamine) and adipic acid (hexanedioic acid) are heated together; the \(\mathrm{-NH_2}\) group of one monomer and the \(\mathrm{-COOH}\) group of the other combine with the loss of a water molecule at every link, forming amide linkages:

\(n\,\mathrm{H_2N-(CH_2)_6-NH_2} + n\,\mathrm{HOOC-(CH_2)_4-COOH} \xrightarrow{\Delta} [-\mathrm{HN-(CH_2)_6-NH-CO-(CH_2)_4-CO}-]_n + 2n\,\mathrm{H_2O}\)

Each monomer contains SIX carbon atoms, which is why the polymer is named nylon 6,6. It is a polyamide, and the hydrogen bonding between the amide linkages of neighbouring chains is what gives nylon its strength; it is used for fibres, ropes, tyre cord and bristles.

C. ANTACIDS

Antacids are substances taken to neutralise the excess hydrochloric acid secreted in the stomach, so relieving hyperacidity and the pain of an acid stomach. Sodium hydrogencarbonate, magnesium hydroxide (milk of magnesia) and aluminium hydroxide are common antacids and act by direct neutralisation; drugs such as ranitidine and omeprazole act differently, by suppressing the secretion of the acid itself.

D. TWO SIDE EFFECTS OF TRANQUILIZERS

1. They depress the central nervous system, so they cause drowsiness, dullness and loss of alertness and muscular coordination.

2. They are habit forming, so continued use leads to dependence and to withdrawal symptoms when the drug is stopped.

answer:
**(A)** Ethylamine

The reaction described is the carbylamine reaction. On warming with chloroform (a haloform) and alcoholic potassium hydroxide, a PRIMARY amine gives a foul, offensive smelling alkyl isocyanide, also called a carbylamine:

\(\mathrm{R-NH_2} + \mathrm{CHCl_3} + 3\mathrm{KOH} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{R-NC} + 3\mathrm{KCl} + 3\mathrm{H_2O}\)

The reaction uses up BOTH hydrogen atoms of the \(\mathrm{-NH_2}\) group, so only an amine that has two hydrogen atoms on nitrogen - that is, a primary amine - can give it. Secondary and tertiary amines do not give this test, which is why it is used to detect a primary amine.

Classifying the four amines by the number of groups attached to nitrogen: ethylamine \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-NH_2}\) carries one group and is primary; diethylamine \(\mathrm{(C_2H_5)_2NH}\) and ethylmethylamine \(\mathrm{C_2H_5-NH-CH_3}\) each carry two and are secondary; triethylamine \(\mathrm{(C_2H_5)_3N}\) carries three and is tertiary. Ethylamine is the only primary amine among them.

\(\therefore\) ethylamine gives the foul smelling product:

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-NH_2} + \mathrm{CHCl_3} + 3\mathrm{KOH} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-NC} + 3\mathrm{KCl} + 3\mathrm{H_2O}\)

The product is ethyl isocyanide.

i. CHLOROFORM AND CAUSTIC POTASH - the carbylamine reaction.

Ethylamine is a primary amine, so on warming with chloroform and alcoholic potassium hydroxide (caustic potash) it gives a foul, offensive smelling isocyanide:

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-NH_2} + \mathrm{CHCl_3} + 3\mathrm{KOH} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-NC} + 3\mathrm{KCl} + 3\mathrm{H_2O}\)

The product is ethyl isocyanide (ethyl carbylamine). Both hydrogen atoms of the \(\mathrm{-NH_2}\) group are used up in the reaction, which is why only primary amines respond and why the reaction serves as a test for them.

ii. NITROUS ACID.

Nitrous acid is unstable, so it is generated in the reaction mixture from sodium nitrite and dilute hydrochloric acid at \(273\text{-}278\ \mathrm{K}\). Ethylamine, being an ALIPHATIC primary amine, first forms an ethyl diazonium salt, but this salt is very unstable and decomposes immediately with the solvent water:

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-NH_2} + \mathrm{HNO_2} \xrightarrow[(\mathrm{NaNO_2 + HCl})]{273\text{-}278\ \mathrm{K}} [\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-N_2^{\oplus}Cl^{\ominus}}] \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_2O}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-OH} + \mathrm{N_2}\uparrow + \mathrm{HCl}\)

Ethanol is obtained and nitrogen gas is liberated with brisk effervescence. The steady stream of nitrogen is the observation that identifies an aliphatic primary amine.

Ethyl cyanide is \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-C}\equiv\mathrm{N}\) (propanenitrile). Sodium with ethyl alcohol supplies nascent hydrogen, which adds across the carbon-nitrogen triple bond. This is the Mendius reduction:

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-C}\equiv\mathrm{N} + 4[\mathrm{H}] \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Na/C_2H_5OH}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH_2-NH_2}\)

The reduction product is PROPYLAMINE (propan-1-amine), \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH_2-NH_2}\), a primary amine.

Counting the carbon atoms: the nitrile carbon is RETAINED and becomes the carbon that carries the amino group, so the amine has one carbon atom MORE than the alkyl group of the cyanide. Ethyl cyanide has three carbon atoms in all and propylamine also has three, which is the check that the product is right.

The same reduction is brought about by \(\mathrm{LiAlH_4}\) or by hydrogen over a nickel catalyst.

answer:
In the carbylamine reaction a PRIMARY amine is heated with chloroform and alcoholic potassium hydroxide and gives a foul, offensive smelling alkyl isocyanide, also called a carbylamine. The general equation is

\(\mathrm{R-NH_2} + \mathrm{CHCl_3} + 3\mathrm{KOH} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{R-NC} + 3\mathrm{KCl} + 3\mathrm{H_2O}\)

For ethylamine, \(\mathrm{R} = \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-}\):

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-NH_2} + \mathrm{CHCl_3} + 3\mathrm{KOH} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-NC} + 3\mathrm{KCl} + 3\mathrm{H_2O}\)

The product is ethyl isocyanide (ethyl carbylamine), \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-NC}\), and its offensive smell is what makes the reaction easy to observe.

Both hydrogen atoms of the \(\mathrm{-NH_2}\) group are consumed in the reaction, so only a primary amine can give it; secondary and tertiary amines do not. The reaction is therefore used as a test for primary amines, aliphatic and aromatic alike.

answer:
Name of the reagent: SILVER NITRITE.

Formula: \(\mathrm{AgNO_2}\).

An alkyl halide warmed with silver nitrite gives the nitroalkane, the silver halide separating out:

\(\mathrm{R-X} + \mathrm{AgNO_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{R-NO_2} + \mathrm{AgX}\)

For example,

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-Br} + \mathrm{AgNO_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-NO_2} + \mathrm{AgBr}\)

giving nitroethane.

Why silver nitrite and not sodium or potassium nitrite. The nitrite ion is ambident - it can bond to carbon either through its nitrogen atom, giving the nitroalkane \(\mathrm{R-NO_2}\), or through an oxygen atom, giving the alkyl nitrite \(\mathrm{R-O-N=O}\). In silver nitrite the silver-oxygen bond is largely covalent, so the oxygen atoms are tied up and the nitrogen atom is the site available for attack; the NITROALKANE is therefore the main product. Sodium nitrite and potassium nitrite are ionic, the oxygen atoms are free, and attack takes place through oxygen to give the alkyl nitrite instead.

The nitroalkane so obtained is the starting material for one of the preparations of amines: reducing it with tin and hydrochloric acid gives the corresponding primary amine,

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-NO_2} + 6[\mathrm{H}] \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Sn/HCl}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-NH_2} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)

[Note: the Amines chapter takes the nitroalkane as a starting material in its reduction of nitro compounds and does not itself print this preparation of the nitroalkane from the alkyl halide.]

**(D)** 4-Aminobenzoic acid

All four compounds are aromatic amines, so the comparison turns on ONE thing: how available the lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom is for accepting a proton. The more available the lone pair, the stronger the base.

In aniline itself the lone pair on nitrogen is conjugated with the aromatic ring and so is partly delocalised into it, which is why arylamines are weaker bases than ammonia and than aliphatic amines. A substituent on the ring shifts this either way:

- an ELECTRON RELEASING group pushes electron density into the ring, the ring draws less from the nitrogen, the lone pair stays more available, and the base is STRENGTHENED;
- an ELECTRON WITHDRAWING group pulls electron density out of the ring, the ring draws still more from the nitrogen, the lone pair becomes less available, and the base is WEAKENED.

Taking the four compounds in turn:

Dimethoxyaniline carries two \(\mathrm{-OCH_3}\) groups. Oxygen has lone pairs which it releases into the ring by resonance, so the methoxy group is electron releasing.

o-Toluidine carries a \(\mathrm{-CH_3}\) group, which releases electrons by its \(+\mathrm{I}\) effect, so it too is electron releasing.

Benzene-1,4-diamine carries a second \(\mathrm{-NH_2}\) group, which likewise releases electron density into the ring by resonance.

4-Aminobenzoic acid carries a \(\mathrm{-COOH}\) group para to the amino group. The carboxyl group WITHDRAWS electron density, both by its \(-\mathrm{I}\) effect and by resonance, and so drags the lone pair on nitrogen still further into the ring, leaving it least available of the four for protonation. Its acidic \(\mathrm{-COOH}\) group works the same way a second time, by protonating the amino group internally and tying up the lone pair altogether.

\(\therefore\) 4-aminobenzoic acid is the weakest base. It is the ONLY one of the four carrying an electron withdrawing substituent; in the other three the substituent releases electrons into the ring, so in each of them the lone pair on nitrogen is left more available than it is here, and none of them can be the weakest.

**(C)** 3

Methylamine is \(\mathrm{CH_3-NH_2}\), so its nitrogen atom already carries ONE methyl group and two hydrogen atoms. Tetramethylammonium iodide is \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_4N^{\oplus}I^{\ominus}}\), in which the nitrogen atom carries FOUR methyl groups and no hydrogen.

Three more methyl groups have therefore to be attached to nitrogen, and in the alkylation of an amine each mole of methyl iodide attaches exactly one methyl group:

\(\mathrm{CH_3-NH_2} + \mathrm{CH_3I} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{(CH_3)_2NH} + \mathrm{HI}\)

\(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2NH} + \mathrm{CH_3I} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{(CH_3)_3N} + \mathrm{HI}\)

\(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3N} + \mathrm{CH_3I} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{(CH_3)_4N^{\oplus}I^{\ominus}}\)

The primary amine is converted to the secondary amine, then to the tertiary amine, and finally to the quaternary ammonium salt, one mole of methyl iodide being consumed at each of the three steps.

\(\therefore\) 3 moles of methyl iodide are required for 1 mole of methylamine.

The count agrees with the rule for the alkylation of amines: a primary amine consumes three moles of alkyl halide to reach the quaternary ammonium salt, a secondary amine two and a tertiary amine one.

Methylphenylamine has one METHYL group and one PHENYL group attached to the nitrogen atom, with one hydrogen atom left on nitrogen, so it is a SECONDARY amine and a mixed (unsymmetrical) one.

STRUCTURE: \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-NH-CH_3}\)

that is, a benzene ring joined to nitrogen, the nitrogen also carrying one hydrogen atom and one \(\mathrm{-CH_3}\) group. Its molecular formula is \(\mathrm{C_7H_9N}\).

IUPAC NAME: N-Methylaniline (equivalently N-methylbenzenamine).

answer:
WHY AMINES ARE BASIC IN NATURE.

The nitrogen atom of an amine is \(sp^3\) hybridised and uses three of its four hybrid orbitals for bonding; the fourth holds a LONE PAIR of electrons. An amine owes its basic character to this lone pair, which it can donate.

As a Lewis base it donates the lone pair to an electron deficient species, for example

\(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3N{:}} + \mathrm{BF_3} \longrightarrow \mathrm{(CH_3)_3N^{\oplus}-BF_3^{\ominus}}\)

As a Lowry-Bronsted base it accepts a proton from water, so an aqueous solution of an amine contains hydroxide ions and turns red litmus blue:

\(\mathrm{R-NH_2} + \mathrm{H_2O} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{R-NH_3^{\oplus}} + \mathrm{OH^{\ominus}}\)

The alkyl groups attached to nitrogen release electrons by their \(+\mathrm{I}\) effect. This increases the electron density on the nitrogen atom, makes the lone pair more available, and stabilises the positive charge on the substituted ammonium ion that is formed. The better stabilised that conjugate acid, the further to the right the equilibrium lies and the stronger the base.

WHICH OF THE TWO IS MORE BASIC.

Basic strength is measured by \(\mathrm{pK_b}\), and the SMALLER the \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) value, the stronger the base. Here

dimethylamine: \(\mathrm{pK_b} = 3.27\)

diethylamine: \(\mathrm{pK_b} = 3.0\)

and \(3.0 < 3.27\).

\(\therefore\) diethylamine is the more basic of the two.

This agrees with the \(+\mathrm{I}\) effect argument above: an ethyl group releases electrons more strongly than a methyl group, so it puts more electron density on nitrogen and stabilises \(\mathrm{(C_2H_5)_2NH_2^{\oplus}}\) better than the methyl groups stabilise \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2NH_2^{\oplus}}\).
twin: Why are primary aliphatic amines stronger bases than ammonia ?

answer:
**(C)** Diphenylamine

An amine is classified by the NUMBER of alkyl or aryl groups bonded DIRECTLY TO THE NITROGEN ATOM, and not by the nature of the carbon atom that carries the amino group. A secondary amine has two such groups on nitrogen and one hydrogen atom left, giving the imino group \(\mathrm{{>}NH}\).

Taking the four compounds in turn:

Cyclohexylamine \(\mathrm{C_6H_{11}-NH_2}\) has ONE group on nitrogen and two N-H bonds, so it is a primary amine.

Isopropylamine \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2CH-NH_2}\) also has ONE group on nitrogen, so it too is a primary amine - even though the carbon atom carrying the amino group is a secondary carbon. This is exactly the point the classification rule guards against.

Diphenylamine \(\mathrm{(C_6H_5)_2NH}\) has TWO phenyl groups on nitrogen and one hydrogen atom left, so it is a secondary amine.

N,N-Dimethylaniline \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-N(CH_3)_2}\) has THREE groups on nitrogen - one phenyl and two methyl - and no hydrogen atom at all, so it is a tertiary amine.

\(\therefore\) diphenylamine is the secondary amine.

Reading the name in two parts: the parent is ETHANAMINE, \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-NH_2}\), a two carbon chain carrying the amino group; the prefix N,N-dimethyl places TWO methyl groups on the NITROGEN atom, the locant N showing that they sit on nitrogen and not on the carbon chain. Both hydrogen atoms of the \(\mathrm{-NH_2}\) group are thereby replaced.

STRUCTURAL FORMULA:

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-N(CH_3)_2}\)

which may also be written \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-N(CH_3)-CH_3}\).

The nitrogen atom carries one ethyl group and two methyl groups and has no hydrogen atom left, so N,N-dimethylethanamine is a TERTIARY amine. Its molecular formula is \(\mathrm{C_4H_{11}N}\).

Checking the count: three groups on nitrogen means a tertiary amine, and the carbon atoms are \(2 + 1 + 1 = 4\), which agrees with \(\mathrm{C_4H_{11}N}\).

Amines are nitrogen containing organic compounds having basic character.

Structurally they are the derivatives of AMMONIA obtained by replacing one, two or three of the hydrogen atoms of an ammonia molecule by alkyl or aryl groups:

\(\mathrm{NH_3} \longrightarrow \mathrm{R-NH_2}\) (primary amine, the amino group \(\mathrm{-NH_2}\))

\(\mathrm{NH_3} \longrightarrow \mathrm{R_2NH}\) (secondary amine, the imino group \(\mathrm{{>}NH}\))

\(\mathrm{NH_3} \longrightarrow \mathrm{R_3N}\) (tertiary amine)

The nitrogen atom retains its lone pair of electrons in every one of these, and it is that lone pair which makes amines basic - it is donated to a proton or to an electron deficient species.

Examples: ethylamine \(\mathrm{C_2H_5-NH_2}\), dimethylamine \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2NH}\), trimethylamine \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3N}\) and aniline \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-NH_2}\).

Amines are widespread in nature; they occur in proteins, vitamins, hormones and in plant products such as nicotine, and many medicines are amines.

**(A)** Amide

An acid anhydride is an ACYLATING agent, and a primary amine has two replaceable, positively polarised hydrogen atoms on its nitrogen atom. In acylation one of these N-H hydrogen atoms is replaced by an acyl group, and the compound formed carries the \(\mathrm{-CO-NH-}\) linkage, that is, the AMIDE functional group. The reaction is carried out in the presence of a base such as pyridine, which takes up the carboxylic acid produced.

\(\mathrm{R-NH_2} + \mathrm{(CH_3CO)_2O} \xrightarrow{\text{pyridine}} \mathrm{R-NH-CO-CH_3} + \mathrm{CH_3COOH}\)

For ethylamine and acetic anhydride:

\(\mathrm{C_2H_5-NH_2} + \mathrm{(CH_3CO)_2O} \xrightarrow{\text{pyridine}} \mathrm{C_2H_5-NH-CO-CH_3} + \mathrm{CH_3COOH}\)

The product is N-ethylethanamide (N-ethylacetamide), an N-substituted amide.

The other functional groups offered can be ruled out from the same equation. A nitrile would need a carbon-nitrogen triple bond \(\mathrm{-C}\equiv\mathrm{N}\) and an imine a carbon-nitrogen double bond \(\mathrm{{>}C=N-}\); acylation forms neither, since the nitrogen keeps its single bonds throughout. Nor is a secondary amine formed: the acyl group \(\mathrm{-CO-CH_3}\), not an alkyl group, becomes attached to nitrogen, and the amide so formed is far less basic than the parent amine because the lone pair on nitrogen is drawn into the carbonyl group.

\(\therefore\) the product contains the amide functional group.
